lead.en: A self-proclaimed brother of Christ challenges the Qing

summary.en: Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the brother of Christ, rose against the Qing and founded the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom with its capital at Nanjing. The civil war killed an estimated 20 to 30 million people, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 19th century.

lead.en: In 20 years the colonies' population nearly quadrupled

summary.en: In February 1851 Edward Hargraves, back from the California diggings, panned gold near Bathurst. Later that year even richer fields were found at Ballarat and Bendigo in Victoria. Diggers poured in from around the world: the colonies' population grew from about 430,000 in 1851 to 1.7 million in 1871. Gold made Melbourne one of the richest cities of the empire.

title.en: The Great Exhibition and the first public toilets

lead.en: 827,000 visitors pay a penny for the first public flush toilet

summary.en: At the 1851 Great Exhibition in the Crystal Palace, George Jennings installed the first modern public flush toilets. 827,280 visitors paid a penny each to use them, which is why the British still say 'spend a penny' for going to the loo.

lead.en: The bend 'from Nicholas I's finger' was built 26 years later

summary.en: The line opened on 1 November 1851, and its straightness spawned a legend: Nicholas I drew it with a ruler, his pencil skirted his finger, and builders dutifully added a bend. In fact the Verebye bypass was built only in 1877 to avoid a steep 17-km gradient.

lead.en: American steamships' guns force open a closed Japan

summary.en: In July 1853 four American ships under Commodore Matthew Perry, smoking and painted black, entered Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open to trade. Perry returned half a year later with a stronger squadron, and in March 1854 the shogunate signed the Convention of Kanagawa, opening two ports. Japan's two centuries of seclusion were over, and the shogunate itself soon fell.

lead.en: Sevastopol falls and Russia loses its Black Sea fleet

summary.en: In 1853–1856 Russia fought the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France and Sardinia. After a 349-day siege Sevastopol fell, and under the Treaty of Paris Russia lost the right to keep a navy in the Black Sea.

title.en: New Year's dinner inside an Iguanodon

lead.en: Scientists dine inside the mould of a dinosaur statue

summary.en: On New Year's Eve 1853 the sculptor Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins held a dinner party inside the mould of his Iguanodon. His Crystal Palace models were the world's first life-size dinosaur sculptures, and wildly wrong by today's standards: only three of the 15 genera are true dinosaurs.

lead.en: Gold miners under the Southern Cross demanded the vote

summary.en: Ballarat's diggers, angered by costly licences and police raids, built a timber stockade and raised a blue flag bearing the Southern Cross. At dawn on 3 December 1854 soldiers took it within minutes; at least 27 people died, most of them miners. Yet juries acquitted everyone charged with treason, licences were abolished, and rebel leader Peter Lalor soon sat in parliament.

lead.en: A European first sees the great falls of the Zambezi

summary.en: In November 1855 the Scottish missionary David Livingstone, crossing Africa along the Zambezi, became the first European to see the falls locally called Mosi-oa-Tunya and named them after Queen Victoria. His journeys spurred European interest in the African interior.

lead.en: The US Army imports camels to tame the Wild West

summary.en: On 14 May 1856, 34 camels bought by the US Army in the Middle East were unloaded in Texas; one had died on the voyage, but two were born. They coped superbly with the Southwest's deserts, yet the Army never adopted them, and after the Civil War they were auctioned off.

lead.en: He sought a malaria cure and got a fashionable purple

summary.en: Over the Easter holiday, 18-year-old student William Perkin tried to make quinine from coal tar and got a black sludge that dyed cloth a brilliant purple. It was the first synthetic dye, and it made Perkin rich.

lead.en: India passes from the Company to direct Crown rule

summary.en: In May 1857 sepoys, Indian soldiers of the East India Company, mutinied at Meerut, and revolt spread across northern and central India. After it was crushed, Company rule was abolished and India passed under the direct rule of the British Crown.

lead.en: The Thames reeks so badly Parliament considers fleeing

summary.en: In the hot summer of 1858 the sewage in the Thames stank so badly that Parliament's curtains were soaked in chloride of lime and MPs discussed moving to Oxford. The stench finally pushed through Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system, which still serves London.

title.en: Darwin's On the Origin of Species

lead.en: Natural selection explains the diversity of life

summary.en: In November 1859 Charles Darwin published his book on the origin of species by means of natural selection. The theory of evolution explained the diversity of life by natural processes, provoked fierce debate and became the foundation of modern biology.

lead.en: A bankrupt merchant declares himself Emperor of the US

summary.en: In 1859 the bankrupt merchant Joshua Norton proclaimed himself 'Emperor of the United States'. San Francisco played along: restaurants accepted his own banknotes, and one of his 'decrees' called for a bridge to Oakland, which opened in 1936.

lead.en: A shot pig nearly starts a war between the US and Britain

summary.en: In 1859 an American farmer on disputed San Juan Island shot a British-owned pig rooting in his potatoes. Both sides brought in troops and warships, but no more shots were fired: the pig remained the only casualty.

lead.en: A solar storm let telegraphs run without batteries

summary.en: On 1 September 1859 astronomer Richard Carrington saw a brilliant flare on the Sun; within a day the strongest geomagnetic storm on record hit Earth. Auroras lit up the tropics, telegraphs sparked, and some lines ran with their batteries disconnected, on current induced by the storm.

lead.en: Horseback mail across half a continent lasts 18 months

summary.en: From April 1860 Pony Express riders carried mail from Missouri to California in about 10 days, changing horses at relay stations. But in October 1861 the telegraph linked the coasts, and two days later the company announced its closure.

lead.en: Garibaldi and Cavour forge a single kingdom

summary.en: After Garibaldi's campaigns and the wars engineered by Prime Minister Cavour, the Kingdom of Italy under Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed in Turin. Unification was completed with Venice in 1866 and Rome in 1870.

title.en: Emancipation of the serfs in Russia

lead.en: Millions of peasants gain personal freedom

summary.en: On 19 February (3 March) 1861 Alexander II signed the manifesto freeing the serfs. More than 20 million privately owned peasants gained personal freedom but had to pay redemption for their land. The reform opened Russia's era of Great Reforms.

lead.en: The Union survives and slavery is abolished

summary.en: The war between the Union and the seceded slaveholding states of the Confederacy began with the bombardment of Fort Sumter in April 1861. The Union victory preserved the United States, and the 13th Amendment of 1865 abolished slavery nationwide.

lead.en: Lincoln declares slaves in the rebel states free

summary.en: On 1 January 1863, in the middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln declared free the slaves in the territories in rebellion against the Union. The proclamation turned the war into a fight to end slavery and opened the Union army to Black soldiers. The 13th Amendment abolished slavery throughout the United States in 1865.

lead.en: Tens of thousands of islanders tricked onto plantations

place.en: Queensland and the islands of Melanesia

summary.en: From 1863 recruiters brought people from Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands and other archipelagos to Queensland's sugar plantations. Some signed contracts they did not understand; others were lured aboard or kidnapped outright, hence the slang "blackbirding". Some 62,000 islanders were taken to Queensland. After 1901 the new Australian federation deported most of them.

title.en: End of the Caucasian War and the Circassian expulsion

lead.en: Hundreds of thousands of Circassians are driven to the Ottomans

summary.en: On 21 May 1864 a parade at Kbaada (today Krasnaya Polyana) marked Russia's end of the Caucasian War. Most Circassians (Adyghe), the native people of the north-western Caucasus, were forced off their land: hundreds of thousands left for the Ottoman Empire, and many died of hunger and disease on the coast and on the way. Their descendants now live in Turkey, Jordan and Syria; in Russia, as the Adyghe, Kabardians and Cherkess.

lead.en: The bloodiest war in Latin American history

summary.en: Dictator Francisco Solano López drew Paraguay into war against the Triple Alliance of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay. For six years the Paraguayans fought to the bitter end; the war ended only with López's death at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870. By various estimates the country lost between a quarter and more than half of its population, including most adult men.

lead.en: The shot at Ford's Theatre five days after victory

summary.en: On 14 April 1865, five days after the main Confederate army surrendered, the actor John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre. The president died the next morning, the first US president to be assassinated.

lead.en: A monk found the laws of heredity, and nobody noticed

summary.en: Augustinian friar Gregor Mendel spent eight years crossing peas in his monastery garden and worked out the laws of heredity. A local natural history journal printed his paper, which went almost uncited for 34 years until three botanists independently rediscovered it in 1900.

lead.en: Russia cedes its North American territory to the United States

summary.en: On 30 March 1867 Russia signed a treaty selling Alaska to the United States for $7.2 million. The territory was formally transferred on 18 October 1867 at Sitka (New Archangel).

lead.en: Canada is born without a war, by an act of Parliament

summary.en: On 1 July 1867 the British North America Act came into force: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick united as the Dominion of Canada, with Ottawa as its capital. John A. Macdonald became the first prime minister. Manitoba and British Columbia soon joined, and 1 July is celebrated as Canada Day.

title.en: Ee ja nai ka: dancing at the end of the shogunate

lead.en: Amulets fall from the sky and Japan breaks into dance

summary.en: In 1867–68, as the Tokugawa shogunate crumbled, days-long carnivals swept Japan after sacred amulets reportedly fell from the sky. People cross-dressed, danced in the streets and chanted 'Ee ja nai ka!' — roughly 'Why not?'

lead.en: A boy picks up a shiny pebble and starts a diamond rush

summary.en: In 1867 fifteen-year-old Erasmus Jacobs found a shiny pebble by the Orange River. It was a 21-carat diamond, the first authenticated in South Africa. The find set off the Kimberley diamond rush and made the region the world's great source of diamonds.

lead.en: Isolated Japan races to become a world power

summary.en: In 1868 the Tokugawa shogunate was abolished and power formally returned to Emperor Meiji. Japan, until recently closed to the outside world, carried out Western-style reforms and within decades became an industrial and military power.

lead.en: Ships from Europe to Asia no longer round Africa

summary.en: On 17 November 1869 the Suez Canal, built under Ferdinand de Lesseps, was opened. Linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, it spared ships the voyage around Africa and dramatically shortened the route from Europe to Asia.

lead.en: An epic of the Napoleonic wars — a summit of the novel

summary.en: In 1869 the final volume of Leo Tolstoy's epic, written at his Yasnaya Polyana estate, was published. Its panorama of Russian society during the Napoleonic Wars is counted among the greatest novels in world literature.

lead.en: A golden spike joins two oceans

summary.en: On 10 May 1869 the tracks of the Central Pacific, built from the west, and the Union Pacific, built from the east, met in Utah, and a ceremonial golden spike was driven in. The line across the Sierra Nevada was laid mainly by thousands of Chinese workers. Crossing from the Atlantic to the Pacific shrank from months to about a week.

lead.en: Empty squares predict elements yet to be found

summary.en: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known chemical elements by atomic weight and properties into a periodic system. He left gaps in his table and predicted the properties of undiscovered elements, gallium, scandium and germanium, which were soon found.

lead.en: Napoleon III offers a prize for a butter substitute

summary.en: Napoleon III offered a prize for a cheap butter substitute for the army and the poor. In 1869 the chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès won it with “oleomargarine”, made from beef fat and milk.

lead.en: Defeat at Sedan topples Napoleon III's empire

summary.en: In July 1870 France declared war on Prussia but was quickly defeated: on 2 September Napoleon III himself was captured at Sedan and France became a republic. Paris surrendered after a siege in January 1871. Victory let Bismarck unify Germany, while France lost Alsace and part of Lorraine.

lead.en: Bismarck forges a new great power at Versailles

summary.en: On 18 January 1871, after victory over France, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Unification under Otto von Bismarck created a new great power at the heart of Europe.

lead.en: Workers rule Paris for two months, then die in the Bloody Week

summary.en: After France's defeat by Prussia, Parisians rose in March 1871 and set up the Commune, a revolutionary city government. In late May Versailles troops retook the city, killing thousands of Communards.

lead.en: Stanley's famous line was most likely invented later

summary.en: On 10 November 1871 the New York Herald reporter Henry Stanley found the missing explorer David Livingstone at Ujiji. 'Dr Livingstone, I presume?' is not in his journal: the two pages after the meeting were torn out, and historians think he made the line up later.

title.en: O’Keefe and the stone money of Yap

lead.en: An Irish captain gets rich shipping stone money

summary.en: In 1871 the Irish-American David O’Keefe washed up on Yap. He began shipping huge stone discs, Yap’s money, from Palau on his own vessel, was paid in copra, and became known as the island’s “king”.

lead.en: Artists rejected by the Salon give a new movement its name

summary.en: In April 1874 Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Morisot and others rejected by the official Salon exhibited in photographer Nadar's former studio. A critic mocked them as 'Impressionists' after Monet's Impression, Sunrise, and the name stuck.

lead.en: Bell sends a voice down a wire — the world starts calling

summary.en: In March 1876 Alexander Graham Bell was granted a patent for the telephone and days later spoke the first words over a wire to his assistant. Long-distance voice communication transformed business, daily life and government.

lead.en: Drought kills millions while grain is still exported

summary.en: After the monsoons failed during a powerful El Niño, drought gripped southern and western India. By various estimates 5.5 to 10 million people died of hunger and disease. The colonial authorities cut relief and did not halt grain exports, and at the height of the disaster, in 1877, Viceroy Lytton held a lavish Delhi Durbar to proclaim Victoria Empress of India.

lead.en: The empire's first constitution lasted just over a year

summary.en: On 23 December 1876 Sultan Abdul Hamid II, pressed by reformers led by Midhat Pasha, proclaimed a constitution. The first parliament, with Muslim, Christian and Jewish deputies, met in 1877. But in February 1878, amid war with Russia, the sultan suspended it and ruled alone for another 30 years.

lead.en: A simple arc lamp lights the streets of Paris and London

summary.en: Russian engineer Pavel Yablochkov patented in Paris a simple arc lamp needing no regulator, the 'electric candle'. It lit streets in Paris, London and St Petersburg, and this 'Russian light' became the first mass electric street lighting.

lead.en: Custer's Last Stand fell on the day the telephone was shown

summary.en: On 25–26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse routed the 7th Cavalry. Lt Col Custer and every man with him were killed; on the same day the telephone was being demonstrated in Philadelphia.

lead.en: Tchaikovsky's flop becomes the world's most famous ballet

summary.en: On 4 March 1877 Pyotr Tchaikovsky's ballet premiered at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre. The first staging was not a success, but the 1895 Petipa–Ivanov production at the Mariinsky made Swan Lake the world's most famous ballet.

lead.en: A translation slip gave Mars its canal-building Martians

summary.en: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped a network of dark lines on Mars and called them canali, 'channels'. English readers took it as 'canals', something built, and for decades the public believed in Martian engineers. The lines turned out to be an optical illusion.

lead.en: Europe redraws the Balkans after the Russo-Turkish War

summary.en: Under Bismarck's chairmanship the Great Powers revised the outcome of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78. Serbia, Montenegro and Romania became independent, Bulgaria autonomous, and Russia lost part of its gains.

lead.en: An obelisk sailed in an iron tube and was lost in a storm

summary.en: Gifted to Britain back in 1819, the obelisk was towed from Alexandria inside an iron cylinder-ship. In October 1877 it had to be cut loose in a Biscay storm; Spanish fishermen found it four days later, and in 1878 the Needle was raised on the Thames.

lead.en: A carbon filament and a power grid light up cities

summary.en: In October 1879 a carbon-filament lamp burned for over 13 hours in Thomas Edison's laboratory. Building on predecessors such as Lodygin and Swan, Edison produced a practical bulb and a power-distribution system that lit up cities.

lead.en: Spear-armed Zulus deal Britain one of its worst defeats

summary.en: On 22 January 1879 some 20,000 Zulu warriors fell on a British camp below Isandlwana hill. Deployed in the traditional 'horns of the buffalo', they surrounded and killed more than 1,300 rifle-armed British troops and allies. It was the British army's worst defeat by an indigenous force. Even so, the Zulu kingdom was crushed six months later at Ulundi.

lead.en: A war over nitrates left Bolivia landlocked

summary.en: A dispute over taxes on nitrate mining in the Atacama Desert pitted Chile against Bolivia and its ally Peru in 1879. Chile's navy won control of the sea, and in 1881 its army entered Lima. Chile took the nitrate-rich provinces, and Bolivia lost its coastline, a loss it still regards as a national wound.

lead.en: Australian outlaws fight in armour made of ploughs

summary.en: In 1880 bushranger Ned Kelly's gang faced the police at Glenrowan in homemade bulletproof armour beaten from plough mouldboards; the police had dismissed a tip-off about it as preposterous. Kelly alone of the gang survived the 12-hour siege and was hanged.

lead.en: A People's Will bomb kills the tsar and ends the reform era

summary.en: On 13 March 1881 members of Narodnaya Volya threw bombs at the carriage of Emperor Alexander II. The tsar who had freed the serfs was mortally wounded; his successor Alexander III reversed the course of reform.

lead.en: The Wild West's most famous gunfight lasted 30 seconds

summary.en: On 26 October 1881 the Earp brothers and Doc Holliday faced a gang of Cowboys in Tombstone. About thirty shots were fired in thirty seconds, and not at the O.K. Corral at all but in a narrow lot by a photo studio, six doors from its rear entrance.

lead.en: Hawaii's king becomes the first monarch to circle the globe

summary.en: In 1881 Hawaii's King Kalākaua travelled around the world in 281 days, the first monarch ever to do so. He visited Japan, China, Siam, India, Egypt and Europe seeking plantation workers, and on the way home called on Edison to see electric light.

lead.en: Gaudí's basilica has been under construction for nearly 150 years

summary.en: Work on the Basilica of the Holy Family began in 1882, and a year later Antoni Gaudí took over, devoting the rest of his life to it. Funded by donations, construction continues to this day.

lead.en: A blast heard 4,800 km away, and tsunamis sweep away villages

summary.en: On 27 August 1883 Krakatoa exploded with a bang heard 4,800 km away, and tsunamis wiped out hundreds of coastal villages, killing over 36,000 people. For several years, unusually vivid red sunsets were seen around the world.

lead.en: The half-striped zebra dies in a zoo, almost unnoticed

summary.en: On 12 August 1883 the last quagga, a South African zebra striped only on its front half, died in Amsterdam's zoo. Settlers had shot out the wild population for hides and meat. Two weeks before Krakatoa erupted, hardly anyone noticed.

lead.en: Europe carves up Africa with no Africans present

summary.en: European powers and the United States met in Berlin at Bismarck's invitation to set rules for colonising Africa. The conference, with no Africans present, accelerated the Scramble for Africa: by 1914 nearly the whole continent was divided among colonial powers.

title.en: Founding of the Indian National Congress

lead.en: 72 delegates in Bombay begin India's road to independence

summary.en: In December 1885, 72 delegates from across British India met in Bombay for the first session of the Indian National Congress, initiated by a retired British official, Allan Octavian Hume. At first the Congress modestly asked for more Indians in government. Within decades, under Gandhi and Nehru, it led the mass movement that brought India independence in 1947.

lead.en: The British relief force arrives just two days too late

summary.en: The Sudanese preacher Muhammad Ahmad, proclaiming himself the Mahdi, rose against Egyptian-British rule. After a ten-month siege his fighters stormed Khartoum on 26 January 1885 and killed General Charles Gordon; the British relief force arrived two days later. The Mahdist state lasted until 1898, when its army was mown down by machine guns at Omdurman.

lead.en: A Belgian king's private domain built on rubber and terror

summary.en: In 1885 the vast Congo basin became the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium. To extract rubber and ivory, people were forced into labour and punished for missed quotas, even by having hands cut off. By various estimates the population fell by millions. After Roger Casement's exposés and an international outcry, Belgium took the colony from the king in 1908.

lead.en: Inside the egg a yolk, inside the yolk a hen, inside it a crown

summary.en: At Easter 1885 Alexander III gave his wife an enamel egg by Fabergé: inside was a gold 'yolk', inside that a ruby-eyed hen, and inside the hen a tiny crown and pendant. The empress was so delighted that the tsar ordered a new surprise egg for every Easter after.

lead.en: A petrol engine replaces the horse

summary.en: On 29 January 1886 Karl Benz patented his three-wheeled petrol-driven Motorwagen, the first practical automobile. In 1888 Bertha Benz drove it over 100 km, proving its worth and launching the age of the car.

lead.en: A tent camp grows into Johannesburg within a decade

summary.en: In 1886 the outcrop of the planet's richest gold reef was found on the Langlaagte farm in the Boer republic of the Transvaal. A prospectors' camp grew into Johannesburg, home to some 100,000 people a decade later. By estimates, around 40% of all gold ever mined has come from the Witwatersrand. The struggle for this wealth led to the Anglo-Boer War of 1899.

title.en: The first Coca-Cola sold in a pharmacy

lead.en: A pharmacist sells a 'temperance drink' made with coca

summary.en: When Atlanta went dry, pharmacist John Pemberton made a non-alcoholic version of his coca wine. On 8 May 1886 Jacob's Pharmacy sold the first Coca-Cola at five cents a glass, as a patent medicine. Its key ingredients were cocaine from coca leaves and caffeine from kola nuts.

lead.en: An imported plague kills up to 90% of cattle, starving herders

summary.en: Around 1887 rinderpest reached Eritrea with Asian cattle imported to feed Italian troops. Within a decade it swept to southern Africa, killing an estimated 90% of cattle and countless wild grazers. Famine ravaged Ethiopia and East African herders at the height of the Scramble for Africa.

title.en: Golden Law abolishes slavery in Brazil

lead.en: The last country in the Americas to abolish slavery

summary.en: On 13 May 1888 Princess Regent Isabel signed a law of two short articles abolishing slavery with no compensation. By various estimates around 700,000 people were freed. Over three centuries Brazil had received more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas. Resentful planters turned against the monarchy, which was overthrown a year and a half later.

lead.en: A temporary fair attraction becomes the symbol of Paris

summary.en: Gustave Eiffel's 300-metre tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair, marking the centenary of the Revolution. It was due to be dismantled after 20 years but was saved by its use as a radio antenna.

lead.en: The view from an asylum window becomes an iconic painting

summary.en: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Rémy, where he had admitted himself. He considered it a failure; today it hangs in New York's Museum of Modern Art.

lead.en: An army doctor goes to Java seeking the 'missing link'

summary.en: The Dutch doctor Eugène Dubois joined the colonial army in order to hunt for human ancestors in the East Indies. In 1891, on the Solo River near Trinil, his workers found a skullcap, and a year later a thighbone. Dubois named the creature Pithecanthropus erectus, the 'upright ape-man'; today the finds are assigned to Homo erectus.

lead.en: Rails link Moscow to the Pacific

summary.en: In 1891 construction of the Great Siberian Route began at Vladivostok. The world's longest railway, stretching over 9,000 km from Moscow to the Pacific, tied European Russia to Siberia and the Far East.

lead.en: All Persia quits smoking to kill a British concession

summary.en: Naser al-Din Shah granted a Briton a monopoly on all Iranian tobacco. In 1891 the cleric Shirazi issued a fatwa against tobacco, and a country that smoked even in mosques stopped; even the women of the shah's harem reportedly quit. The concession was cancelled in January 1892.

title.en: New Zealand women win the vote

lead.en: First self-governing country where women vote nationally

summary.en: On 19 September 1893 the governor signed the Electoral Act, making New Zealand the first self-governing country where women could vote in parliamentary elections. The campaign was led by Kate Sheppard; that year's petitions gathered nearly 32,000 signatures. Ten weeks later, on 28 November, about two-thirds of the country's women voted, Māori women included. They could not stand for parliament until 1919.

lead.en: Planters and US Marines took the throne from a queen

summary.en: On 17 January 1893 a "Committee of Safety" of American and European businessmen deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani, who had planned a new constitution. Marines landed from the cruiser USS Boston left her no chance, and she yielded to avoid bloodshed. Sanford Dole headed the new republic, and in 1898 the US annexed the islands. A century later Congress formally apologised for the coup.

lead.en: Navy money goes on a stone ship that cannot sail

summary.en: In 1893 Empress Dowager Cixi had a pavilion in the Summer Palace rebuilt as a paddle steamer, wooden but painted to look like marble. The palace was restored largely with money meant for a new navy, and the stone boat that cannot sail is seen as a bitter irony.

title.en: Court rules the tomato a vegetable

lead.en: The US Supreme Court rules on whether a tomato is a fruit

summary.en: A tomato importer argued that tomatoes were fruit and exempt from the duty on vegetables; botanically, they are berries. In 1893 the US Supreme Court disagreed: people serve tomatoes with dinner, not dessert, so they are vegetables.

lead.en: A modernised Japan defeats the Qing Empire

summary.en: The war began over control of Korea, where the Donghak peasant rebellion had broken out. Japan's army and navy, rebuilt on Western lines, routed Qing forces at Pyongyang and the Qing fleet off the Yalu. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 China recognised Korea's independence, ceded Taiwan to Japan and paid a huge indemnity. The balance of power in Asia was overturned.

lead.en: The Black Death's microbe is found in a straw hut

summary.en: The third plague pandemic spread from China's Yunnan province and in 1894 reached Hong Kong, from where shipping carried it around the world. In June 1894 the Swiss-French doctor Alexandre Yersin, working in a hastily built hut, isolated the bacterium later named Yersinia pestis. By estimates the pandemic killed more than 12 million people, most of them in India.

lead.en: Invisible rays let doctors see inside the body

summary.en: On 8 November 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered invisible rays that pass through flesh. An image of his wife's hand amazed the world and within a year the rays were used in medicine. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

lead.en: A device catches radio waves — Russia's Radio Day

summary.en: On 7 May 1895 Alexander Popov demonstrated a receiver of electromagnetic waves to the Russian Physical and Chemical Society. The day is celebrated in Russia as Radio Day; Guglielmo Marconi was developing wireless telegraphy in parallel.

lead.en: The first paid film screening — cinema is born

summary.en: On 28 December 1895, at the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines, Auguste and Louis Lumière held the first paid public screening of films with their Cinématographe. The date is widely regarded as the birth of cinema.

lead.en: Russia's most 'ancient' souvenir dates only from the 1890s

summary.en: The first matryoshka was turned in the 1890s by Vasily Zvyozdochkin to a design by the painter Sergey Malyutin of the Mamontovs' Abramtsevo circle. The set had eight dolls, the largest holding a rooster. In 1900 it won a bronze medal at the Paris World's Fair and became a symbol of Russia.

lead.en: Asia's first anti-colonial revolution

summary.en: In August 1896 the secret society Katipunan, led by Andrés Bonifacio, rose against three centuries of Spanish rule. In December the Spanish executed the writer José Rizal, who became a national martyr. On 12 June 1898 Emilio Aguinaldo proclaimed the independence of the Philippines, but under the Treaty of Paris the islands passed to the United States.

lead.en: Menelik II routs Italy and keeps Ethiopia free

summary.en: On 1 March 1896 the army of Ethiopian Emperor Menelik II routed an Italian invasion force. Ethiopia kept its independence and became one of only two African states to escape colonisation during the Scramble for Africa.

lead.en: Coubertin revives the ancient games in Athens

summary.en: In April 1896 Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games, revived on the initiative of Pierre de Coubertin. Athletes from 14 nations competed, with events held in the restored ancient Panathenaic Stadium.

title.en: An opera house in the Amazon

lead.en: Rubber barons build an opera house in the jungle

summary.en: Rubber-boom money built an opera house in Manaus, deep in the rainforest, which opened in 1896. Its roof tiles came from Alsace, its steel from Glasgow and its marble from Carrara, and the dome is clad in 36,000 tiles in the colours of the Brazilian flag.

lead.en: The shortest war in history: under an hour

summary.en: On 25 August 1896 the Sultan of Zanzibar died and Khalid bin Barghash took the throne without the British consul's approval. Britain issued an ultimatum; when it expired at 9 a.m. on 27 August, its ships shelled the palace. The war lasted 38 to 45 minutes, the shortest on record.

lead.en: Thousands of Benin Bronzes end up in Europe's museums

summary.en: In February 1897 a British punitive expedition of some 1,200 men took the capital of the Kingdom of Benin in reprisal for the killing of a British mission. The city burned, Oba Ovonramwen was exiled, and thousands of bronze plaques and carved tusks were carried off and sold. Today the Benin Bronzes symbolise the restitution debate: in 2022 Germany transferred ownership of more than a thousand pieces to Nigeria.

lead.en: The Maine explodes in Havana, and Spain's empire ends

summary.en: On 15 February 1898 the US battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, and American newspapers demanded war with Spain, which was fighting Cuban rebels. The fighting lasted less than four months, and the Spanish fleet was destroyed off Santiago de Cuba. Spain ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the US, and Cuba gained independence under American tutelage.

lead.en: Its suppression hastens the fall of the Qing dynasty

summary.en: The secret society of the Boxers rose against foreigners and Christians and besieged Beijing's Legation Quarter. An Eight-Nation Alliance crushed the revolt and imposed a huge indemnity on China, hastening the fall of the Qing.

lead.en: The first car to top 100 km/h was electric

summary.en: On 29 April 1899 Belgian Camille Jenatzy drove his torpedo-shaped electric car to 105.88 km/h, the first time any car had passed 100 km/h. He named it La Jamais Contente, 'The Never Satisfied'.

lead.en: Nobel's will creates the top award in science and letters

summary.en: On 10 December 1901, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace were awarded for the first time under his will. The Nobel Prize became the most prestigious award in science and culture.

lead.en: Six colonies unite into one nation

summary.en: On 1 January 1901 six British colonies united as the Commonwealth of Australia, proclaimed in Sydney's Centennial Park. Edmund Barton became the first prime minister. Australia gained a common constitution and parliament as a dominion of the British Empire.

title.en: Annie Taylor goes over Niagara in a barrel

lead.en: A 63-year-old teacher is the first to survive Niagara in a barrel

summary.en: On 24 October 1901, her 63rd birthday, schoolteacher Annie Taylor climbed into a barrel with a heart-shaped pillow and went over Niagara Falls, the first person ever to survive it. The barrel had been tested on a cat beforehand, which survived too.

lead.en: A light bulb burning in a fire station since 1901

summary.en: A carbon-filament bulb, now glowing at about 4 watts, was hung in a Livermore fire station in 1901 and has hardly been switched off since. It is in Guinness World Records, and a webcam lets anyone watch it.

lead.en: A searing cloud erases the 'Paris of the Caribbean' in minutes

summary.en: On 8 May 1902 a glowing cloud of gas and ash destroyed Saint-Pierre, the 'Paris of the Caribbean', in minutes, killing about 28,000 people. Among the very few survivors was prisoner Ludger Sylbaris, shielded by the thick walls of his cell.

lead.en: Twelve seconds aloft launch the age of aviation

summary.en: On 17 December 1903 Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first controlled, sustained flight in a powered aeroplane. The first attempt lasted just 12 seconds but opened the age of aviation, which within half a century transformed war, travel and the world.

title.en: N-rays: a discovery that never was

lead.en: Scores of scientists studied rays that did not exist

summary.en: Physicist René Blondlot of Nancy announced a new kind of radiation and named it after his home town. Dozens of scientists confirmed it, until American Robert Wood secretly pocketed a key prism from the apparatus and Blondlot went on 'seeing' the rays.

lead.en: The 20th century's first genocide, in German South West Africa

summary.en: In 1904 the Herero and Nama rose against German colonists. After the Battle of Waterberg, General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order: the Herero were driven into the Omaheke desert and cut off from waterholes, and survivors were sent to concentration camps. By various estimates up to 65,000 Herero and about 10,000 Nama died. Germany officially recognised it as genocide in 2021.

lead.en: Defeat at Tsushima hastens revolution in Russia

summary.en: The war over Manchuria and Korea began with a Japanese naval attack on Port Arthur. After the fortress fell and the Battle of Tsushima, Russia accepted defeat in the Treaty of Portsmouth. Japan's victory stunned Europe and helped spark Russia's 1905 revolution.

lead.en: The US sends seven warships to Morocco for one hostage

summary.en: In 1904 the chieftain Raisuni kidnapped the wealthy American Ion Perdicaris in Tangier. Theodore Roosevelt sent seven warships, and Secretary of State Hay declared 'Perdicaris alive or Raisuli dead'. The Sultan met the kidnapper's demands, and the furore helped Roosevelt win re-election.

lead.en: The leader rides in a car, the champion is fed rat poison

summary.en: The first man home in the 1904 Olympic marathon, Fred Lorz, had ridden part of the way in a car. The real winner, Thomas Hicks, was dosed with strychnine, brandy and egg by his trainers and almost carried over the line. Cuba's Andarín Carvajal ate rotten apples and took a nap mid-race.

lead.en: A patent clerk's four papers lay the base of modern physics

summary.en: In 1905 patent clerk Albert Einstein published four papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and mass–energy equivalence (E = mc²). Together they laid the foundations of modern physics.

lead.en: After Bloody Sunday, the tsar grants a Duma and civil liberties

summary.en: The shooting of peaceful marchers on 22 January 1905, 'Bloody Sunday', set off a wave of strikes and revolts. The October Manifesto granted civil liberties and created the State Duma, Russia's first parliament.

lead.en: Merchants and clerics force the shah to share power

summary.en: Protests in 1905 against arbitrary rule and foreign concessions grew into a mass strike, with thousands of Tehranis taking refuge in the grounds of the British legation. In 1906 Mozaffar ad-Din Shah granted a constitution and the first Majlis opened. In 1908 the new shah shelled parliament, but in 1909 constitutionalists took Tehran and deposed him.

lead.en: Shaking and fires destroy 80% of the city and teach seismology

summary.en: On 18 April 1906 the San Andreas Fault ruptured for hundreds of kilometres. The quake and fires that raged for days destroyed about 80% of San Francisco and killed some 3,000 people. Studies of the disaster helped explain how earthquakes occur.

lead.en: A gusher in the Persian hills opens the region's oil age

summary.en: On 26 May 1908, after seven fruitless years of drilling under William Knox D'Arcy's concession, geologist George Reynolds struck a gusher. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company — the future BP — was founded a year later. The Royal Navy soon switched from coal to oil, and the Middle East became the world's chief oil reservoir.

lead.en: A cosmic blast flattens 2,150 km² of Siberian forest

summary.en: On 30 June 1908 a cosmic body, probably an asteroid or comet fragment, exploded over the Siberian taiga. The blast flattened forest over some 2,150 km², and night skies over Europe glowed for days. Leonid Kulik's first expedition reached the site only in 1927.

lead.en: Conspirator officers force the sultan to restore the constitution

summary.en: In summer 1908 officers of the secret Committee of Union and Progress mutinied in Macedonia. Fearing an army revolt, Abdul Hamid II restored the 1876 constitution on 24 July amid public jubilation. A year later the sultan was deposed, and power gradually passed to the committee's leaders, Enver, Talaat and Djemal.

lead.en: A Sicilian city in ruins — Russian sailors are first to help

summary.en: On 28 December 1908 an earthquake and tsunami levelled Messina and Reggio Calabria, killing an estimated 75,000 to 120,000 people. Sailors of a Russian naval squadron nearby were among the first rescuers and are still remembered in Messina.

lead.en: Díaz's fall leads to land reform and workers' rights

summary.en: A revolt against the long-ruling dictator Porfirio Díaz grew into a civil war involving Madero, Zapata, Villa and Carranza, costing hundreds of thousands of lives. The 1917 constitution proclaimed land reform and workers' rights.

title.en: Earth passes through Halley's Comet's tail

lead.en: Newspapers spread panic as hucksters sell 'comet pills'

summary.en: In May 1910 Earth passed through the tail of Halley's Comet. Press reports of astronomer Camille Flammarion's remarks about poisonous cyanogen in the tail caused panic, and hucksters sold 'comet pills' and gas masks. Nothing happened.

lead.en: The fall of the Qing ends imperial China

summary.en: The Wuchang Uprising of 10 October 1911 led to the fall of the Qing dynasty. The Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 January 1912 under Sun Yat-sen, and the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in February, ending over two thousand years of imperial rule.

lead.en: Norwegians beat Scott in the race to the Pole

summary.en: On 14 December 1911 Roald Amundsen's Norwegian expedition became the first to reach the South Pole. Robert Falcon Scott's British party arrived five weeks later and perished on the return. The race became a symbol of the heroic age of polar exploration.

title.en: The theft of the Mona Lisa

lead.en: A Louvre handyman took it; Picasso was questioned

summary.en: On 21 August 1911 former Louvre worker Vincenzo Peruggia, in a staff smock, walked out with the Mona Lisa. The poet Apollinaire and Pablo Picasso were detained, and the painting turned up only in 1913 in Florence. The press frenzy made it the most famous painting in the world.

lead.en: The Ottomans lose almost all of Europe — a prelude to world war

summary.en: In 1912 Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece and Montenegro routed the Ottoman Empire, then fell out over the spoils in 1913. The quarrel over Macedonia and Serbia's rise helped bring on the First World War.

title.en: The death of Scott's polar party

lead.en: Amundsen's tent awaited them at the Pole, then death

summary.en: On 17 January 1912 Robert Falcon Scott and four companions reached the South Pole and found the Norwegian flag: Amundsen had beaten them by five weeks. All five died on the return march from cold, hunger and exhaustion. The last three were found in their tent in November 1912, about 18 km from a supply depot. Scott's diary made their fate one of the best-known stories of polar exploration.

lead.en: The “unsinkable” liner sinks after hitting an iceberg

summary.en: On the night of 15 April 1912 the Titanic, the largest liner of its day, on its maiden voyage from Southampton to New York, struck an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic. About 1,500 people died: there were lifeboats for only half of those on board. The disaster led to the first international convention on safety of life at sea.

lead.en: Cars built in 90 minutes — motoring goes mass-market

summary.en: In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line at Highland Park. Assembly time for a Model T fell from about 12 hours to 90 minutes, cars became affordable to the masses, and the line became the emblem of industrial mass production.

lead.en: Phalke's silent epic gives birth to Indian cinema

summary.en: In 1913 Bombay saw the premiere of Dadasaheb Phalke's silent film Raja Harishchandra, based on a story from Indian epic tradition. It is regarded as the first full-length Indian feature film and launched what became one of the world's largest film industries.

title.en: Tagore wins the Nobel Prize for Gitanjali

lead.en: First non-European laureate opens Indian letters to the West

summary.en: In 1913 Bengali poet Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his collection Gitanjali. He was the first non-European to receive the literature prize, introducing Indian literature to Western readers.

lead.en: The first plane with a cabin, a bedroom and a toilet

summary.en: In 1913 Igor Sikorsky built a four-engined plane with a heated cabin, wicker chairs, a bedroom, electric light and history's first airborne toilet. In February 1914 it carried a record 16 passengers, but war broke out and the Muromets became bombers.
